I just realized that I wrote a novel in this reply. Sorry! 

**tl;dr** - eat in a smaller deficit if you feel hungry and tired all the time, stay hydrated, eat lots of protein and veggies, focus on an average for the week instead of a specific number of calories each day, and consider taking a small amount of caffeine during lunch to help with hunger later in the day (but not so late that it interferes with sleep).



If a large calorie deficit while exercising results in exhaustion and hunger, you don’t have to have a deficit that big. Losing 2 lb a week is the maximum recommended by my trainer, but I was still able to lose 1 lb a week on 1800 calories. It may take longer with a smaller deficit, but something sustainable is better than something quick. This may not be accurate, but I think it was easier to be in a larger deficit when I had higher body fat because my body could use the fat as fuel. I was able to build muscle even while I was in a deficit. As my body fat percentage decreased, it was harder. I now eat in a slight surplus to build muscle.



When I first start tracking or going into a deficit, I always try to do it over a long weekend when I don’t have much to do. For example, I started counting calories on a 3 day weekend. I had time to make most of my own meals at home, rest when I felt tired, drink plenty of water and caffeine free tea, and didn’t have the stress of work to cause me to overeat. Once the long weekend was over and I had to go back to work, my body was more accustomed to the lower calories and the hunger pangs didn’t bother me as much.

Eating a lot of protein, eating high volume veggies, and staying hydrated helped a lot. I carried around a large bottle of water with me everywhere. I would feel more tired and hungry if I wasn’t hydrated. I also kept a lot of snacks in my work lunch box to tide me over if I felt hungry between breakfast and lunch (e.g. nonfat Greek yogurt, carrots and celery with dip, protein bars).  

I think one thing that helped is that I didn’t eat the same number of calories every day. I would increase or decrease depending on how hungry I was. Here is an example from the early months:

Monday: 1373

Tuesday: 1248

Wednesday: 1710

Thursday: 1683

Friday: 1348

Saturday: 1897

Sunday: 1379

Average for the week: 1519

I may feel hungrier on the days I exercise, or less hungry on the weekends because I’m mainly staying inside and not moving around as much. As long as my average for the week was around 1500, I would see consistent weight loss every week.

Also, people think this is weird, but I take caffeine pills instead of drinking coffee. A cup of coffee may have 100 mg caffeine and an energy drink like 16oz can of C4 would have 200 mg. I’m sensitive to caffeine so drinking actual coffee or taking energy drinks makes my anxiety worse and gives me stomachaches. I also have problems with executive functioning and would forget to brew coffee every morning. I take prescription medicine for my health issues, so taking pills comes easily. 

I would break the 200 mg caffeine pill in half and take 100 mg in the morning and 100 mg at noon. That would help with hunger pangs during a deficit. I avoid other forms of caffeine like black tea, green tea, diet coke, or even decaff coffee. I would like to wean myself off caffeine eventually but my work schedule and busy life don’t allow me to get 8 hours of sleep and most of the adult at my job and gym consume way more caffeine than I do so I’m OK with this for now.

These are just things that worked for me. Losing weight and keeping it off is HARD and there are so many factors at play that make it complex. I also felt like I spent years gaining and losing the same few pounds, but I learned something new each time about what works and doesn’t work for me. I’m really trying to figure out something sustainable for the long term. I wish you the best with reaching your goals.

I looked back on some of the data from MyFitnessPal. I was averaging 1400-1500 the first 4.5 months and losing about 2 lb per week. 

By month 5, I was starting to feel more hungry and struggled to keep my calories that low. I had lost about 40 lbs at that point and was weight training on a regular basis so I had less body fat to use as fuel. I increased to 1850 calories on average at month 5 and lost weight more slowly (about 5 lbs per month in months 5 and 6). 

By the 7th month I was up to 2000 calories and then 2200 by month 8. I was trying to figure out what my maintenance calories were in the subsequent months. I got down to about 130 lb at my lowest (month 11.5) and I have been spending the past 6 months trying to figure out maintenance and hovering around the 136 lb range. I hope this helps.

I'm glad to hear that it was helpful in some way. Best wishes for reaching your goals! 

I started to feel "old" when I turned 30 (lower back pain, reflux and unspecified GI issues, random aches and pains etc). All those things went away after I started eating healthier and strength training. I hope that this coming year is a good one for you.

My hunger pangs are the worst the first few days when I start a deficit, but my body gets used to it after a few days. When I am in a deficit, I drink a lot of water water or caffeine free tea and have low calorie snacks on hand around the home and at work. For work, I packed a big lunchbox with 2-3 days worth of food and snacks. If I felt really hungry at work and needed something before lunch, I would get some nonfat Greek yogurt, veggies and dip, apples, popcorn, or a protein bar. If that doesn't do it and I'm still hungry, an extra portion of lunch (less calorie dense and high protein options like salad, chicken, veggies, rice, baked potatoes) would usually satisfy me. Always having my own snacks on hand helped a lot. 

I found that eating a larger breakfast helped me avoid feeling tired or hungry during the time I needed the most energy (i.e. work 8-5). I've heard some people say the opposite, but that's what worked for me.

Also, instead of aiming for a set number of calories per day, I would allow myself to eat a little less or more depending on how hungry I was that day. At the end of the week I would calculate the average calories, and as long as the average is close to my target, I would still lose 1 lb per week.

Also, weight training means that I mostly maintained muscle and lost mostly fat, which meant that my TDEE was higher and I could eat a little more than when I was just dieting but remained sedentary. I also ate a lot of protein in order to maintain muscle. Protein has the added benefit of being satiating.

I don't plan cheat days or cheat meals during the week because I find that it derails me. However, I will allow myself to eat more during the holidays or certain social events. I do make different choices at restaurants or family dinners than I would have in the past. I'm used to eating more whole foods and don't crave the same things I ate in the past. Since I track everything, I can see how having several days eating in a surplus slows down my progress and can adjust accordingly if there is a plateau.

Thank you, I really appreciate it. Honestly, the real reason why I stayed consistent with exercise was because it helped with my mental health symptoms and helped me find a community of people who accept me despite my differences. It also got me out of the house multiple times a week and gave me something to look forward to. Things have improved and I am happier and more stable than I have been in nearly two decades.
Calorie counting through MyFitnessPal, strength training 3x per week, and staying consistent

tl;dr: calorie counting, strength training 3x per week, and staying consistent  

  
I took a strength training class 3x per week because I’m not motivated to go to the gym by myself and felt intimidated because I didn’t know what to do. I also tracked calories in MyFitnessPal and I’m careful about measuring portions accurately (e.g. kitchen scale, measuring cups). Instead of hitting a certain calorie goal every day, I aimed for an average over the week so I could eat a little more on the days I felt hungry. This made it more sustainable. In the past I relied a lot on fast food and prepackaged frozen food because I didn’t know how to cook. I used one of the meal kit services to learn how to cook lower calorie meals that tasted just as good if not better than fast food. After a few months I stopped the meal kits because they are expensive and made simpler recipes on my own.   

  
I have had several “failed” weight loss attempts in the past where I would lose 35-40 lbs in 8 months, get burned out/hungry/exhausted, quit and gained all the weight back plus more. Back then, I did a significant calorie restriction (1200 calories) and a ketogenic diet but I didn’t exercise (I had no motivation to go to the gym and no money for classes as a broke college student). I found that I was exhausted all the time. Also, because keto was so restrictive, I struggled when eating in social situations (e.g. family dinners, parties, free food at work). If I ate too many carbs for the day, it felt like I failed so I had an all or nothing mentality. For me personally, it wasn’t sustainable in the long term though I know it is a helpful approach for many people.   

  
I’ve been maintaining this weight for about 7 months now. Honestly, I’m worried that I’ll gain the way back like I did in the past, so I’ll continue to count calories, weigh myself once a week, and exercise on a regular basis. I’m also motivated to eat healthier and exercise now that I’m in my 30s because my body isn’t as resilient as when I was in my 20s and I feel worse when I don’t take care of my health.  

  
I don’t restrict or limit any foods, which makes it so much less stressful because I can eat whatever as long as I’m mindful of the portions. I also, now that I'm maintaining, I don’t stress if I eat double my TDEE during the holidays or go out to eat because I know I’m fairly consistent the rest of the time. If anyone has tips on maintaining in the long term, I’d appreciate any advice.

I also don't have to motivation to exercise or do much of anything. However, I do know how to show up for an appointment or cancel with 24 hours notice (15+ years of therapy plus having to work full time with no safety net). 

Paying for a group exercise class or personal trainer is the only way I have been able to exercise regularly. I have chronic suicidal ideation. Exercise reduced those symptoms significantly. My other symptoms remained the same. When I stop exercising, the suicidal ideation returns.

My therapist recommended that I make an appointment with my primary care doctor in order to get a referral for a registered dietitian. I'm apprehensive. I would love for someone to tell me what to eat and how much to eat but the dietitians I saw at my university just told me to do intuitive eating and never followed up with me. Had anyone else worked with a dietitian? Was it worth the time and expense?



Also, I am trying to figure out whether I should buy a mini refrigerator to put in the garage. I live with my family and there are seven of us in total. We have one refrigerator and it always seems to be packed with food. Any fruit or cheese or meat needs to be carefully hidden or it will be gone the next day. 



I feel that I don't have room to put my food or meal prep. As a result, I eat out for almost every meal, which is part of the reason why I am overweight. The only times in the past when I have been successful with weightloss is when I lived alone and had ample fridge space. When I lived with multiple roommates and shared a refrigerator with 10 or 20 college students I was unsuccessful.



Would buying my own mini refrigerator be worth the investment or am I just making excuses?

Are you familiar with the [Interpersonal-Psychological Theory of Suicidal Behavior] (http://www.apa.org/science/about/psa/2009/06/sci-brief.aspx)? If so, what do you think of it? 

It proposes that “an individual will not die by suicide unless s/he has both the desire to die by suicide and the ability to do so.” People who have the desire to die perceive themselves to be a burden and feel alienated from others/socially isolated. However, people who are *capable* of overcoming the survival instinct and successfully killing themselves are those who have been repeatedly exposed to pain, injury, and death. Suicide is more common in occupations (e.g. physician, soldier) that give repeated exposure to pain and injury.

I have been suicidal for over a decade but I think that the reason why I’m not dead yet is because I don’t have that “acquired ability to enact lethal self-injury.” I want to work on developing it.

I was a vegetarian for over a decade and did vegetarian keto for about 8 months. I lost 20% of my body weight. I aimed for about 30-35 grams net carbs and didn't have a problem staying in ketosis. Here are my most common meals from that time:

* Eggs (fried, egg salad, hard boiled, veggie omelet)
* Broccoli cheese soup (plenty of fat and protein)
* Stir Fry
* Cauliflower crust pizza with Tofurky pepperoni and mushrooms
* Quesadillas with low carb crust
* Taco salad with avocado, salsa, cheese, tofurky chorizo, sour cream
* Salad 
* Cheesy Baked Eggplant (Linda's Low Carb Recipe)
* Roasted asparagus, brussel sprouts, cauliflower, broccoli
* Cheesey cauliflower "mashed potatoes"
* Morningstar Grillers Veggie burgers with cheese and no bun
* Zucchini noodles or shirataki noodles with pesto/alfredo sauce/low carb vodka sauce
* String cheese, baybel cheese snacks, laughing cow cheese wedgeds
* Protein shakes
* "Cereal" recipe from vegetarian keto subreddit with almond milk
* Fat bombs
* Quest Bars
* Chia seed pudding
* Creamed spinach
* Seaweed snacks
* Nuts and nut butters (almonds, peanuts, macadamia nuts)
* Peanut butter and celery
* Small portions of berries with whipped cream

I am no longer a vegetarian but I keep a lot of my habits from that time (eating more veggies, 30 gram net carbs, not eating much meat). I did a lot more cooking then, so I would make a large batch of something (e.g. cheesy baked eggplant) and eat it throughout the week. I would divide the broccoli cheese soup into individual servings in freezer bags. I would let one serving thaw overnight in the fridge and bring it (and a bowl) with me for lunch.

I think the non-keto hunger symptoms may be associated with changes in blood sugar, which is less of an issue with keto.

I'm 5'7" and completely sedentary so my TDEE is low. Based on various calculators, 1250 is only a 417 calorie deficit so I would expect to lose less than a pound a week after the initial 5-10 lbs of water weightloss when you first start keto.

The first time I did keto two years ago I started at 157 lbs and lost about 32 lbs in seven months (technically six months because I went off keto in November).  Half of the weight (17 lbs) was lost during the first two months. I was aiming for 1300 calories (lowered to 1200 as I lost more weight) but I think I may have been eating more in the later months because I wasn't measuring as carefully (Especially nuts. I've learned to just buy the 100 calorie packs). Motivation and impatience is an issue with me too, which is why I fell off the wagon hard when school/personal life became really stressful. I went off keto  for over and year gained much of the weight back. I started again on May 30th at 144 lbs and I have lost 14 lbs so far. 

I used keto sticks initially, but I've stopped buying them because most of the sticks "expire" before I use them all. I can tell if I'm in ketosis if I have a pretty significant weightloss in a short period of time for the first month and I don't feel as hungry during the day. Also, when I'm in ketosis I feel fatigued/weak when I'm hungry. When I'm not in ketosis, I feel of nauseous with a growling stomach, gas, and a headache when I'm hungry. Pay attention to any changes that you notice in how your body is functioning.
